hints: Focus on what concentrated sulfuric acid can do besides acting as an acid, it can also take electrons from other species.
Both salts first make their hydrogen halide, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HBr}$, but only $\text{HBr}$ goes on to be oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$ with $\text{SO}_2$ also formed.
Ask yourself which halide ion gives up electrons more easily, and what that tells you about relative reducing strength.
walkthrough:
**Spot the first reaction that happens for both salts**

Both reactions start as a simple acid-base displacement. The stronger non-volatile acid displaces the more volatile acid.

$$\text{NaX(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HX(g)}$$ where $\text{X = Cl or Br}$

**See what happens next with the hydrogen halide**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is also a strong oxidising agent. It is strong enough to oxidise $\text{HBr}$ to bromine, but not strong enough to oxidise $\text{HCl}$ to chlorine.

$$\text{2HBr + H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O}$$

**Link this to reducing agent strength**

If $\text{Br}^-$ is oxidised but $\text{Cl}^-$ is not by the same oxidising agent, $\text{Br}^-$ must lose electrons more easily. That means bromide is the stronger reducing agent, which explains the extra products like $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$ only with $\text{NaBr}$.

options.A: Volatility explains why HX leaves the mixture, but both HCl and HBr are volatile. It does not explain why HBr is oxidised to Br2 while HCl is not.
options.B: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, not a weak acid, and it is fully dissociated in water. Acid strength is not the reason for the different redox behaviour here.
options.C: This statement is incorrect. Concentrated sulfuric acid is a good oxidising agent, which is exactly why it oxidises HBr to Br2 while being reduced to SO2.
options.D: Bromide ion loses electrons more readily than chloride ion, so it reduces concentrated H2SO4 to SO2 while itself being oxidised to Br2. Chloride is too weak a reducing agent to do this, so the reaction stops at HCl.
